text:
AI Verify — two independent defects
def average_adjusted_price(prices, threshold, discount_rate):
    """Return the average price after applying an eligible discount."""
    adjusted_prices = []

    for price in prices:
        if price > threshold:
            adjusted_prices.append(price - discount_rate)
        else:
            adjusted_prices.append(price)

    total_adjusted_price = 0

    for index in range(len(adjusted_prices) - 1):
        total_adjusted_price += adjusted_prices[index]

    return total_adjusted_price / len(adjusted_prices)
Use prices = [80, 120, 200, 100], threshold = 100, and discount_rate = 0.10.
The intended rule is: values strictly above 100 receive a 10% discount.

Predict the correct adjusted values and average by hand.
Run the AI-generated function.
Diagnose two independent defects:

the rate is treated as a flat amount rather than a proportion;
the final adjusted value is omitted from the accumulated total.

Fix & verify with a second case that contains a value exactly equal to the threshold.

total_revenue = 0

title: Course Guide
text:
The learning model
DSA105 treats programming as a way of making reasoning explicit, executable, and testable.
The recurring classroom cycle is:

Do → Observe → Name → Explain → Do Again

You will rarely remain passive for long periods. Most class segments require a visible action: predict an output, modify code, explain a result, complete a partial implementation, debug a mistake, or build a small solution.

title: Course Guide
text:
Why Python?
Python is used because it turns abstract ideas into concrete outcomes that can be executed immediately.
The relationship is:
Computational idea → Algorithm → Python representation → Output → Verification
Python is therefore both: - a programming language that you must learn to use; and - a concrete surface on which computational reasoning can be tested.

title: Course Guide
text:
Class timing: 14:20–16:40
DSA105 is scheduled as three 40-minute class hours. This gives 120 minutes of effective teaching time within the 14:20–16:40 block.
For TRACE Studio, the block is organized as two longer active-learning sessions:









Clock time
Duration
Phase
Typical student activity




14:20–15:20
60 min
Session 1
retrieval, problem framing, prediction, micro-lecture, guided coding


15:20–15:35
15 min
Break
—


15:35–16:35
60 min
Session 2
guided lab, pair challenge, debugging, domain application, evidence task


16:35–16:40
5 min
Close / transition
exit instruction, submission check, next-step reminder



The two 60-minute sessions preserve the full 120 minutes of instructional activity while reducing fragmentation. The final five minutes are treated as a transition buffer rather than additional teaching time.

Internal rhythm of each 60-minute session
A 60-minute session should still avoid long passive stretches. A typical internal rhythm is:

10–15 min: problem / prediction / retrieval;
10–15 min: focused explanation or live coding;
15–20 min: guided student action;
10–15 min: pair task, debugging, explanation, or evidence capture.

The exact distribution can change by week, but students should normally be required to do something observable at least every 10–15 minutes.


Alternative view: official 40-minute class hours
The same 14:20–16:40 block can also be understood as:

14:20–15:00 — Class hour 1
15:00–15:10 — Break
15:10–15:50 — Class hour 2
15:50–16:00 — Break
16:00–16:40 — Class hour 3

TRACE Studio uses the 60 + 15 + 60 delivery pattern operationally, while remaining equivalent to the same 120 minutes of effective teaching time.

Why verification matters
A program can run and still be logically wrong.
An AI-generated solution can be syntactically correct and still misunderstand the problem.
Your responsibility is therefore not only to obtain code, but to understand and test the computational behaviour.

title: DSA105 · TRACE Studio
text:
Official course objective
The course aims to develop basic computer-based problem-solving skills by focusing on algorithm development, flowcharting, and programming logic. Python is used as the primary implementation language. Students work with data types, control structures, functions, and file operations, with examples connected to economics, business, and data analysis. Through hands-on exercises, students practice designing, implementing, testing, and debugging programs while building a foundation for advanced data structures and algorithmic thinking.

title: DSA105 · TRACE Studio
text:
Learning outcomes
By the end of DSA105, you should be able to:

Define computational problems.
Design algorithms for problem solving.
Translate algorithms into Python code.
Test and debug programs effectively.
Integrate programming with economics and business analytics contexts.







NoteWhat this course is not



This is not a course in memorizing Python commands. Python gives us a visible and executable way to test whether our reasoning is precise enough for a computer.

A problem, computational pattern, or domain scenario is introduced.


2. Action
You predict, trace, modify, complete, or build something in Colab.


3. Evidence
A short quiz, lab task, exit ticket, or homework records what you can do.


4. Feedback
Your evidence is combined into a learning portfolio after the midterm.

Names such as x, v1, or a are useful only when the meaning is genuinely generic or temporary. In domain code, the name should help explain the program.

title: Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
text:
TipThis week’s central question



What changes when one repeated process contains another repeated process?

title: Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
text:
Connection
Week 8 introduced repeated state. Week 9 introduces state at more than one level.
Names now do conceptual work: branch_total describes state that resets for each branch, while company_total describes state that survives across branches.

title: Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
text:
Debug This
An assistant moved branch_total = 0 outside the outer loop:
company_total = 0
branch_total = 0

for branch in range(1, 3):
    for day in range(1, 4):
        daily_sales = float(input("Sales: "))
        branch_total += daily_sales

    company_total += branch_total

print(f"Company total: {company_total:.2f}")
Use:

Branch 1: 100, 120, 80
Branch 2: 90, 110, 130

Do not run yet.

Predict the final value of company_total.
Trace branch_total after each branch.
Explain why the result becomes 930 instead of 630.
Identify which state must reset for each branch.

The problem is state leakage and double counting, not information loss.

title: Week 9 — Patterns inside Patterns
text:
AI Verify
Now examine a different silent bug:
company_total = 0

for branch in range(1, 3):
    branch_total = 0

    for day in range(1, 4):
        daily_sales = float(input("Sales: "))
        branch_total += daily_sales

    company_total = branch_total

print(f"Company total: {company_total:.2f}")
With the same values, the correct total is 630.

Predict the final value.
Run the program.
Diagnose why assignment overwrites prior branch information.
Fix & verify by accumulating rather than replacing.

section: From visible algorithm to idiomatic Python
text:
From visible algorithm to idiomatic Python
First make the algorithm visible:
high_scores = []

for score in scores:
    if score >= threshold:
        high_scores.append(score)
After you can explain that algorithm, Python also allows:
high_scores = [
    score
    for score in scores
    if score >= threshold
]
The shorter form is not automatically better. Use it only when it remains easy to read.

title: Week 11 — Working with Many Things at Once
text:
AI Verify
def remove_low_scores(scores, threshold):
    """Return scores after removing values below the threshold."""
    for score in scores:
        if score < threshold:
            scores.remove(score)

    return scores
For scores = [2, 3, 8, 9, 7, 9] and threshold = 5, the correct result is [8, 9, 7, 9].

Predict which values should remain.
Run the function on a copy of the list.
Diagnose why removing 2 changes what the loop sees next.
Fix & verify by returning a new filtered list.

title: Week 13 — When Programs Go Wrong
text:
TipThis week’s central question



How do we identify the failure mode before trying to repair it?

title: Week 13 — When Programs Go Wrong
Week 13 — When Programs Go Wrong
text:
Connection
Earlier weeks treated debugging as a recurring activity. Week 13 makes failure classification explicit.
Good error handling is precise: it handles an expected failure without hiding a different one.

title: Week 13 — When Programs Go Wrong
Week 13 — When Programs Go Wrong
text:
AI Verify
def safe_divide(numerator, denominator):
    """Return a quotient while handling division by zero."""
    try:
        return numerator / denominator
    except:
        return 0
Test:

safe_divide(10, 2)
safe_divide(10, 0)
safe_divide(10, "two")


Predict what each call should tell you.
Run all three.
Diagnose why returning 0 for every exception hides real programming errors.
Fix & verify by catching only ZeroDivisionError.

The goal is not “never crash.” The goal is to handle the failure you understand without concealing failures you did not intend.
